title: Χερμάδιον
titleEn: The Tongue and the Stone — Iliad 5.217–317
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Aeneas answers Pandarus’ despair: nothing will do but to meet Diomedes with horses and chariot, and he offers to drive the Trojan team, which can pursue and flee at a rush, or else to fight while Pandarus drives. Pandarus says the horses will do better under the driver they know, and that he himself will meet Diomedes with the spear. Sthenelus sees them coming, names the two men, and urges Diomedes to draw back in the chariot. Diomedes refuses: Athena will not let him flinch, and the swift horses will not carry both of the men home. He tells Sthenelus, if he kills them, to hold his own team back and seize Aeneas’ horses, which come from the breed that Zeus gave Tros for Ganymede and that Anchises stole by breeding from it; of six foals he kept four and gave two to Aeneas. Pandarus throws first and hits Diomedes’ shield, and shouts that he has hit him through the flank. Diomedes answers that he missed, and his spear, guided by Athena, goes in beside Pandarus’ nose, cuts his tongue at the root and comes out under his chin. Pandarus falls dead, and his horses shy away. Aeneas leaps down and strides round the body like a lion, and Diomedes heaves a rock that two men of today could not carry and crushes Aeneas’ hip. Aeneas sinks to his knees and darkness covers his eyes, and he would have died had his mother Aphrodite not seen it and wrapped him in a fold of her robe.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Αἰνείας Τρώων ἀγὸς ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aut’ Aineias Trōōn agos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: Him then in turn Aeneas, leader of the Trojans, spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then Aeneas, leader of the Trojans, spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ … ἀντίον ηὔδα is the stock opening of a reply, ‘and to him in turn … spoke, face to face’, and τόν ‘him’ is Pandarus, whose speech closed the last part (the article is a pronoun in Homer). Αἰνείας is Aeneas, and ἀγός ‘leader’ (from ἄγω ‘lead’) makes him Τρώων ἀγός ‘leader of the Trojans’. ἀντίον is ‘face to face’, and ηὔδα is the imperfect of αὐδάω ‘speak’. A new paragraph begins at 217.

sentences.t: μὴ δ’ οὕτως ἀγόρευε·
sentences.tr: mē d’ houtōs agoreue·
sentences.l: “Do not speak so;
sentences.i: “Do not talk like that;
sentences.n: μὴ δ’ is μηδέ ‘and not’, and ἀγόρευε is the present imperative of ἀγορεύω ‘speak’: ‘do not speak so’ is a flat prohibition. Aeneas is answering Pandarus’ complaint that he has no chariot and his vow to burn his bow; the reasons follow in the next lines.

sentences.t:
πάρος δ’ οὐκ ἔσσεται ἄλλως,
πρίν γ’ ἐπὶ νὼ τῷδ’ ἀνδρὶ σὺν ἵπποισιν καὶ ὄχεσφιν
ἀντιβίην ἐλθόντε σὺν ἔντεσι πειρηθῆναι.
sentences.tr:
paros d’ ouk essetai allōs,
prin g’ epi nō tōid’ andri syn hippoisin kai ochesphin
antibiēn elthonte syn entesi peirēthēnai.
sentences.l:
and before it will not be otherwise,
until against this man we two, with horses and with chariot,
in opposition having gone, with armour, have made trial.
sentences.i: It will not be otherwise before the two of us have gone against this man with horses and chariot, in open opposition, in our armour, and made trial of him.
sentences.n: πάρος ‘before’ is answered by πρίν γ’ ‘until’ (which opens the next line), so the sense is ‘nothing else will be done until we have tried him’. ἔσσεται is the future of εἰμί with the doubled σ (Attic ἔσται). νώ ‘we two’ and ἐλθόντε ‘having gone’ are duals, the Greek number for a pair, as is the pair of men throughout this scene. ὄχεσφιν is the -φιν form (an old instrumental), ‘with chariot’, a plural for one vehicle. ἀντιβίην ‘in opposition’ is an adverb, and πειρηθῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive of πειράω ‘make trial’, the man tried being τῷδ’ ἀνδρί, Diomedes.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγ’ ἐμῶν ὀχέων ἐπιβήσεο, ὄφρα ἴδηαι
οἷοι Τρώϊοι ἵπποι ἐπιστάμενοι πεδίοιο
κραιπνὰ μάλ’ ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα διωκέμεν ἠδὲ φέβεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
all’ ag’ emōn ocheōn epibēseo, ophra idēai
hoioi Trōïoi hippoi epistamenoi pedioio
kraipna mal’ entha kai entha diōkemen ēde phebesthai·
sentences.i: But come, mount my chariot, and you will see what sort of horses the Trojans have, how well they know how to rush this way and that over the plain, in pursuit or in flight;
sentences.n: ἐπιβήσεο is the middle imperative of ἐπιβαίνω ‘mount’ (-εο for -ου), which takes the genitive ἐμῶν ὀχέων ‘my chariot’ (ὄχεα is a plural for one vehicle). ἴδηαι is an aorist subjunctive with the epic ending -ηαι (Attic ἴδῃ), ‘you may see’, after ὄφρα. οἷοι ‘of what sort’ opens the indirect question; Τρώϊοι ‘Trojan’ is the adjective, and ἐπιστάμενοι ‘knowing how’ takes the infinitives διωκέμεν ‘to pursue’ and φέβεσθαι ‘to flee’ (-έμεν is the epic infinitive ending), with πεδίοιο ‘over the plain’ a genitive of the ground covered. κραιπνά, a neuter plural used as an adverb, is ‘in a rush’, strengthened by μάλ’ ‘very’; the adjective κραιπνός is ‘rushing’.

sentences.t:
τὼ καὶ νῶϊ πόλιν δὲ σαώσετον, εἴ περ ἂν αὖτε
Ζεὺς ἐπὶ Τυδεΐδῃ Διομήδεϊ κῦδος ὀρέξῃ.
sentences.tr:
tō kai nōï polin de saōseton, ei per an aute
Zeus epi Tydeïdēi Diomēdeï kydos orexēi.
sentences.l:
Those two will bring us two as well safe to the city, even if again
Zeus should grant glory to Tydeus’-son Diomedes.
sentences.i: These two will bring us safe to the city too, even if Zeus should again grant glory to Diomedes, son of Tydeus.
sentences.n: τὼ is the dual of the article used as a pronoun, ‘those two’, the two horses, and they are the subject of the dual verb σαώσετον, the future of σαόω ‘bring safe’ (Attic σῴζω), with νῶϊ ‘us two’ as object; καί means ‘us as well’. πόλιν δέ is πόλινδε, ‘to the city’, with the suffix -δε of direction. εἴ περ ἂν … ὀρέξῃ is ‘even if … should grant’, the aorist subjunctive of ὀρέγω ‘stretch out, hold out’; κῦδος ὀρέξῃ ‘grant glory’ is a phrase that recurs. Τυδεΐδῃ Διομήδεϊ is the dative, ‘to Tydeus’ son Diomedes’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν μάστιγα καὶ ἡνία σιγαλόεντα
δέξαι, ἐγὼ δ’ ἵππων ἀποβήσομαι ὄφρα μάχωμαι·
sentences.tr:
all’ age nyn mastiga kai hēnia sigaloenta
dexai, egō d’ hippōn apobēsomai ophra machōmai·
sentences.l:
But come now, the whip and the glossy reins
take, and I from the horses will step down so that I may fight;
sentences.i: But come now, take the whip and the glossy reins, and I will step down from the horses so that I may fight;
sentences.n: δέξαι is the aorist imperative of δέχομαι ‘receive, take’: Aeneas offers to hand over the driving. μάστιγα is ‘whip’, ἡνία ‘reins’, and σιγαλόεντα ‘glossy’ is the traditional gloss for the sleek leather. ἵππων ἀποβήσομαι is ‘I will step down from the horses’, with a genitive of separation (the horses stand for the chariot they draw). ὄφρα with the subjunctive μάχωμαι gives the purpose, ‘so that I may fight’, on foot.

sentences.t: ἠὲ σὺ τόνδε δέδεξο, μελήσουσιν δ’ ἐμοὶ ἵπποι.
sentences.tr: ēe sy tonde dedexo, melēsousin d’ emoi hippoi.
sentences.l: or else you receive this man, and to me the horses will be a care.”
sentences.i: or else you take him on yourself, and the horses will be my care.”
sentences.n: ἠέ ‘or else’ gives Pandarus the other choice: if he will not hold the reins, he must meet Diomedes himself. δέδεξο is the reduplicated imperative of δέχομαι, ‘receive’ in the sense of meeting an attack; μελήσουσιν ‘will be a care’ is the future of μέλω with ἵπποι ‘horses’ as subject and ἐμοί ‘to me’. Aeneas’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε Λυκάονος ἀγλαὸς υἱός·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe Lykaonos aglaos huios·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed Lycaon’s splendid son:
sentences.i: Then Lycaon’s splendid son spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε is the stock introduction of a reply, ‘and to him in turn he spoke’, with τόν a pronoun and προσέειπε the aorist of προσεῖπον ‘address’. Λυκάονος ἀγλαὸς υἱός ‘Lycaon’s splendid son’ is Pandarus, whom the narrator names by his father (ἀγλαός ‘splendid’). A new paragraph begins at 229.

sentences.t: Αἰνεία σὺ μὲν αὐτὸς ἔχ’ ἡνία καὶ τεὼ ἵππω·
sentences.tr: Aineia sy men autos ech’ hēnia kai teō hippō·
sentences.l: “Aeneas, you yourself hold the reins and your two horses;
sentences.i: “Aeneas, you yourself keep the reins and your own two horses;
sentences.n: Αἰνεία is the vocative. ἔχ’ is ἔχε, the imperative of ἔχω ‘hold’, and τεώ is the Ionic form of σώ ‘your’, here dual to agree with ἵππω ‘two horses’. σὺ μὲν αὐτός ‘you on your part yourself’ is set against the next lines, which say why the team does better in the driver’s own hands.

sentences.t:
μᾶλλον ὑφ’ ἡνιόχῳ εἰωθότι καμπύλον ἅρμα
οἴσετον, εἴ περ ἂν αὖτε φεβώμεθα Τυδέος υἱόν·
sentences.tr:
mallon hyph’ hēniochōi eiōthoti kampylon harma
oiseton, ei per an aute phebōmetha Tydeos huion·
sentences.l:
More, under a charioteer they are accustomed to, the bent chariot
they two will carry, if again we should flee from the son of Tydeus;
sentences.i: The two horses will carry the bent chariot better under the charioteer they are used to, if we should flee again from the son of Tydeus;
sentences.n: μᾶλλον ‘more, rather’ here means ‘better’. ὑφ’ ἡνιόχῳ εἰωθότι is ‘under a charioteer who is accustomed’ (εἰωθότι is the perfect participle of ἔθω ‘be accustomed’), the one the horses know. οἴσετον is a dual future of φέρω ‘carry’, the two horses the unstated subject. εἴ περ ἂν … φεβώμεθα is ‘if ever we should flee’, the subjunctive of φέβομαι ‘flee’. καμπύλον ‘bent’ is the word also used of the bow; Homer does not say which part of the chariot is curved.

sentences.t:
μὴ τὼ μὲν δείσαντε ματήσετον, οὐδ’ ἐθέλητον
ἐκφερέμεν πολέμοιο τεὸν φθόγγον ποθέοντε,
νῶϊ δ’ ἐπαΐξας μεγαθύμου Τυδέος υἱὸς
αὐτώ τε κτείνῃ καὶ ἐλάσσῃ μώνυχας ἵππους.
sentences.tr:
mē tō men deisante matēseton, oud’ ethelēton
ekpheremen polemoio teon phthongon potheonte,
nōï d’ epaïxas megathymou Tydeos huios
autō te kteinēi kai elassēi mōnychas hippous.
sentences.l:
Lest the two, having been afraid, hang back, and be unwilling
to carry us out of the war, longing for your voice,
and on us two, rushing, the son of great-hearted Tydeus
both ourselves should kill and drive off the solid-hoofed horses.
sentences.i: Lest the two horses, afraid, hang back and refuse to carry us out of the fighting because they miss your voice, and the son of great-hearted Tydeus rush upon the two of us and kill us both and drive off the solid-hoofed horses.
sentences.n: μή here introduces a fear, a warning of what might happen, and it takes the subjunctives ματήσετον, ἐθέλητον, κτείνῃ and ἐλάσσῃ (ματήσετον is a short-vowel subjunctive, though the same form could be a future). ματήσετον is dual, ‘the two hang back’, from ματάω, a rare verb traditionally glossed ‘linger, be slack’. ἐκφερέμεν is an infinitive in -έμεν ‘to carry out’, with πολέμοιο ‘out of the war’ and ποθέοντε the dual participle of ποθέω ‘long for, miss’ (the horses missing Pandarus’ voice). ἐπαΐξας is the aorist participle of ἐπαΐσσω ‘rush at’, αὐτώ is dual ‘both of us ourselves’, and μώνυχας ‘solid-hoofed’ (μώνυξ, ‘with an undivided hoof’, from μόνος ‘single’ + ὄνυξ ‘hoof’) is the epithet of horses, whose hoof is undivided, as against the cloven-hoofed ox.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σύ γ’ αὐτὸς ἔλαυνε τέ’ ἅρματα καὶ τεὼ ἵππω,
τὸν δὲ δ’ ἐγὼν ἐπιόντα δεδέξομαι ὀξέϊ δουρί.
sentences.tr:
alla sy g’ autos elaune te’ harmata kai teō hippō,
ton de d’ egōn epionta dedexomai oxeï douri.
sentences.l:
But you yourself drive your chariot and your two horses,
and him, as he comes on, I will receive with the sharp spear.”
sentences.i: No, you yourself drive your chariot and your two horses, and I will meet him as he comes on with my sharp spear.”
sentences.n: ἔλαυνε is the imperative of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’, τέ’ is τεά ‘your’ (neuter plural, elided) with ἅρματα, a plural for one chariot, and τεὼ ἵππω the dual ‘your two horses’. δεδέξομαι is the future of δέχομαι ‘receive’, here meet the attack, picking up Aeneas’ δέδεξο (228). The line prints both δὲ and δ’ after τόν; only one connective is needed for the sense. ὀξέϊ δουρί is ‘with the sharp spear’. Pandarus’ speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσαντες ἐς ἅρματα ποικίλα βάντες
ἐμμεμαῶτ’ ἐπὶ Τυδεΐδῃ ἔχον ὠκέας ἵππους.
sentences.tr:
hōs ara phōnēsantes es harmata poikila bantes
emmemaōt’ epi Tydeïdēi echon ōkeas hippous.
sentences.l:
So then, having spoken, into the intricate chariot having stepped,
eager against Tydeus’-son they held the swift horses.
sentences.i: So they spoke, and mounting the intricate chariot, they eagerly drove their swift horses against the son of Tydeus.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσαντες is ‘so, then, having spoken’, and the two men are the subject throughout: βάντες is the aorist participle of βαίνω ‘step’, so ‘having stepped into the chariot’ (ἅρματα is plural for one chariot, and ποικίλα ‘intricate’ is the house word for worked and decorated things). ἐμμεμαῶτ’ is the dual of the perfect participle of ἐμμέμονα ‘be eager’. ἔχον ὠκέας ἵππους, ‘held the swift horses’, is a stock phrase for driving a team on. A new paragraph begins at 239.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δὲ ἴδε Σθένελος Καπανήϊος ἀγλαὸς υἱός,
αἶψα δὲ Τυδεΐδην ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
tous de ide Sthenelos Kapanēïos aglaos huios,
aipsa de Tydeïdēn epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
And them saw Sthenelus, Capaneus’ splendid son,
and at once to Tydeus’-son winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: Sthenelus, the splendid son of Capaneus, saw them, and at once he spoke winged words to the son of Tydeus:
sentences.n: τούς ‘them’ are Aeneas and Pandarus coming on. ἴδε is the unaugmented aorist of εἶδον ‘saw’. Καπανήϊος is an adjective, ‘Capaneus’’, so Σθένελος Καπανήϊος ἀγλαὸς υἱός is ‘Sthenelus, Capaneus’ splendid son’, the same shape as the formula for Pandarus at 229. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα ‘spoke winged words’ is the stock introduction of a speech, in which the epithet is translated each time. Sthenelus is Diomedes’ companion in the chariot.

sentences.t:
Τυδεΐδη Διόμηδες ἐμῷ κεχαρισμένε θυμῷ,
ἄνδρ’ ὁρόω κρατερὼ ἐπὶ σοὶ μεμαῶτε μάχεσθαι
ἶν’ ἀπέλεθρον ἔχοντας·
sentences.tr:
Tydeïdē Diomēdes emōi kecharismene thymōi,
andr’ horoō kraterō epi soi memaōte machesthai
in’ apelethron echontas·
sentences.i: “Diomedes, son of Tydeus, dear to my heart, I see two strong men eager to fight against you, with immeasurable strength;
sentences.n: Τυδεΐδη Διόμηδες is the vocative, and ἐμῷ κεχαρισμένε θυμῷ is the perfect participle of χαρίζομαι, ‘made welcome to my heart’, a form of address between friends. ὁρόω is ὁράω ‘see’ with the vowels left uncontracted. ἄνδρ’ is ἄνδρε, the dual ‘two men’, with κρατερώ and μεμαῶτε ‘eager’ also dual (μεμαῶτε is from μέμονα). ἶνα is the accusative of ἴς ‘strength’, with ἀπέλεθρον ‘immeasurable’, and the participle ἔχοντας is plural, loosely, after the dual nouns.

sentences.t:
ὃ μὲν τόξων ἐῢ εἰδὼς
Πάνδαρος, υἱὸς δ’ αὖτε Λυκάονος εὔχεται εἶναι·
sentences.tr:
ho men toxōn eÿ eidōs
Pandaros, huios d’ aute Lykaonos euchetai einai·
sentences.l:
the one, well knowing the bow,
Pandarus, and as son of Lycaon he claims to be;
sentences.i: one is Pandarus, who knows the bow well, and he claims to be a son of Lycaon;
sentences.n: ὃ μέν ‘the one’ is answered by Αἰνείας δέ in the next line. τόξων ἐῢ εἰδώς is ‘well knowing the bow’ (εἰδώς is the perfect participle of οἶδα, and τόξα is a plural for one bow). Sthenelus now gives the first man’s name, and υἱὸς … Λυκάονος ‘son of Lycaon’ repeats the phrase used of him at 229. εὔχεται εἶναι is ‘claims to be’, and αὖτε here is ‘and moreover’.

sentences.t:
Αἰνείας δ’ υἱὸς μὲν ἀμύμονος Ἀγχίσαο
εὔχεται ἐκγεγάμεν, μήτηρ δέ οἵ ἐστ’ Ἀφροδίτη.
sentences.tr:
Aineias d’ huios men amymonos Anchisao
euchetai ekgegamen, mētēr de hoi est’ Aphroditē.
sentences.l:
and Aeneas, as son of blameless Anchises,
claims to be born, and his mother is Aphrodite.
sentences.i: and Aeneas claims to be born the son of blameless Anchises, and his mother is Aphrodite.
sentences.n: Αἰνείας is the subject of εὔχεται ‘claims’ with the infinitive ἐκγεγάμεν, the perfect infinitive of ἐκγίγνομαι ‘be born of’. Ἀγχίσαο is the epic genitive in -αο, and ἀμύμων is translated ‘blameless’ by house rule, though what the word means is not known. μήτηρ δέ οἵ ἐστ’ is ‘and his mother is’ (οἵ = ‘to him’). Line 247 is metrically irregular as transmitted: its fifth foot is a spondee (Ἀγ-χί-, a rare shape), and the syllable σα- of Ἀγχίσαο, which opens the sixth foot, has to be counted long.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε δὴ χαζώμεθ’ ἐφ’ ἵππων, μηδέ μοι οὕτω
θῦνε διὰ προμάχων, μή πως φίλον ἦτορ ὀλέσσῃς.
sentences.tr:
all’ age dē chazōmeth’ eph’ hippōn, mēde moi houtō
thyne dia promachōn, mē pōs philon ētor olessēis.
sentences.l:
But come now, let us draw back on the horses, and do not for me so
rush through the front-fighters, lest in some way you lose your dear heart.”
sentences.i: But come now, let us draw back on the horses, and please do not rush so through the front-fighters, or you may somehow lose your life.”
sentences.n: χαζώμεθ’ is the present subjunctive of χάζομαι ‘draw back’, used as a ‘let us’; ἐφ’ ἵππων is ‘on the horses’, meaning ‘in the chariot’. μοι is an ethic dative (‘for me’, ‘please’) with θῦνε, the imperative of θύνω ‘rush’, and προμάχων is ‘front-fighters’. μή πως … ὀλέσσῃς is ‘lest somehow you lose’, the aorist subjunctive of ὄλλυμι ‘destroy, lose’; φίλον ἦτορ ‘dear heart’ is the heart as the seat of life, so the English layer says ‘life’. Sthenelus’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπόδρα ἰδὼν προσέφη κρατερὸς Διομήδης·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ar’ hypodra idōn prosephē krateros Diomēdēs·
sentences.l: Him then with a scowl looking addressed strong Diomedes:
sentences.i: Then strong Diomedes, looking at him with a scowl, spoke to him:
sentences.n: This is the formula for an answer given with a dark look. ὑπόδρα is an adverb, ‘from under (the brows)’, ‘with a scowl’; its derivation is not certain. ἰδών is ‘looking’, προσέφη ‘addressed’, and κρατερός ‘strong’ is Diomedes’ stock epithet here. A new paragraph begins at 251.

sentences.t: μή τι φόβον δ’ ἀγόρευ’, ἐπεὶ οὐδὲ σὲ πεισέμεν οἴω.
sentences.tr: mē ti phobon d’ agoreu’, epei oude se peisemen oiō.
sentences.l: “Not at all of flight speak, since not even you I think will persuade.
sentences.i: “Do not speak to me of flight; I do not think you will persuade me.
sentences.n: μή τι … ἀγόρευ’ is a prohibition (ἀγόρευ’ is the imperative ἀγόρευε), with τι ‘at all’; φόβον is ‘flight’, the running away that fear drives, and δ’ is the connective δέ, too weak to show in English. ἐπεὶ οὐδὲ … οἴω is ‘since I do not think’ (οἴω = ὀΐω), with the future infinitive πεισέμεν (πείθω ‘persuade’) and σέ as its subject: the Greek does not say whom you would persuade, and ‘me’ is the natural supply.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ μοι γενναῖον ἀλυσκάζοντι μάχεσθαι
οὐδὲ καταπτώσσειν·
sentences.tr:
ou gar moi gennaion alyskazonti machesthai
oude kataptōssein·
sentences.l:
For not true to my birth is it for me, dodging, to fight,
nor to cower;
sentences.i: It does not befit my birth to fight by dodging, or to cower;
sentences.n: γενναῖον is ‘true to one’s birth’ (from γένος ‘birth, stock’), a rare word in Homer; the English follows the root so as to keep ‘noble’ for ἀγαυός. μοι is ‘for me’, and ἀλυσκάζοντι, a dative participle agreeing with it, is ‘for one dodging’ (ἀλυσκάζω, from ἀλύσκω ‘avoid, escape’). μάχεσθαι and καταπτώσσειν ‘to cower’ are the infinitives that γενναῖον governs.

sentences.t: ἔτι μοι μένος ἔμπεδόν ἐστιν·
sentences.tr: eti moi menos empedon estin·
sentences.l: still my might is firm;
sentences.i: my might is still firm;
sentences.n: ἔτι μοι μένος ἔμπεδόν ἐστιν is ‘still my might is firm’: μένος is ‘might’ and ἔμπεδος ‘firm, steady’. Diomedes was hit in the shoulder earlier in this book, and he says his strength has not been taken from him.

sentences.t:
ὀκνείω δ’ ἵππων ἐπιβαινέμεν, ἀλλὰ καὶ αὔτως
ἀντίον εἶμ’ αὐτῶν·
sentences.tr:
okneiō d’ hippōn epibainemen, alla kai autōs
antion eim’ autōn·
sentences.l:
and I shrink from mounting the horses, but just so,
face to face, I will go against them;
sentences.i: I shrink from getting onto the horses, and instead I will meet them face to face just as I am;
sentences.n: ὀκνείω is ὀκνέω ‘shrink from’ with the vowels left uncontracted, and it governs the infinitive ἐπιβαινέμεν (-έμεν) ‘to mount’, with ἵππων in the genitive. ἀλλὰ καὶ αὔτως is ‘but even so, just as I am’, on foot. ἀντίον εἶμ’ αὐτῶν is ‘I will go face to face with them’: εἶμι ‘I shall go’ is a future in sense, and αὐτῶν is the two men.

sentences.t: τρεῖν μ’ οὐκ ἐᾷ Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη.
sentences.tr: trein m’ ouk eāi Pallas Athēnē.
sentences.l: to tremble Pallas Athena does not allow me.
sentences.i: Pallas Athena does not allow me to flinch.
sentences.n: τρεῖν is the infinitive of τρέω, ‘tremble’ or ‘flee in fear’ (the verb covers both, and Homer does not choose), and ἐᾷ is ἐάω ‘allow’ with μ’ (με) as its object. Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη ‘Pallas Athena’ is her stock name; it is her help, given at the start of this book, that Diomedes means.

sentences.t:
τούτω δ’ οὐ πάλιν αὖτις ἀποίσετον ὠκέες ἵπποι
ἄμφω ἀφ’ ἡμείων, εἴ γ’ οὖν ἕτερός γε φύγῃσιν.
sentences.tr:
toutō d’ ou palin autis apoiseton ōkees hippoi
amphō aph’ hēmeiōn, ei g’ oun heteros ge phygēisin.
sentences.l:
And these two, back again, will not carry off, the swift horses,
both from us, if at any rate one of the two escapes.
sentences.i: The swift horses will not carry both of these two back from us, if even one of them escapes.
sentences.n: τούτω is dual ‘these two’ (the men) and is the object of ἀποίσετον, the dual future of ἀποφέρω ‘carry off’, with ὠκέες ἵπποι ‘the swift horses’ as its subject; πάλιν αὖτις ‘back again’ doubles the idea. ἄμφω ‘both’ stands with τούτω, and ἀφ’ ἡμείων is ἀφ’ ἡμῶν ‘from us’ with the epic genitive. εἴ γ’ οὖν ἕτερός γε φύγῃσιν is ‘if at least one of the two should escape’ (ἕτερος ‘one of two’, and φύγῃσιν the subjunctive with the epic ending -σιν).

sentences.t: ἄλλο δέ τοι ἐρέω, σὺ δ’ ἐνὶ φρεσὶ βάλλεο σῇσιν·
sentences.tr: allo de toi ereō, sy d’ eni phresi balleo sēisin·
sentences.l: And another thing to you I will say, and you in your own mind lay it:
sentences.i: And I will tell you something else; lay it up in your own mind:
sentences.n: ἄλλο … ἐρέω is ‘I will tell something else’, where ἐρέω is the epic future of εἶπον and τοι is ‘to you’. βάλλεο is the middle imperative of βάλλω, ‘put for yourself’ (-εο for -ου), σῇσιν is the epic dative plural of σός ‘your own’, and ἐνὶ φρεσί is ‘in your mind’. The line is a formula for an instruction to be remembered, and it stands earlier in the poem too.

sentences.t:
αἴ κέν μοι πολύβουλος Ἀθήνη κῦδος ὀρέξῃ
ἀμφοτέρω κτεῖναι,
sentences.tr:
ai ken moi polyboulos Athēnē kydos orexēi
amphoterō kteinai,
sentences.l:
If to me Athena of many plans should grant glory
both to kill,
sentences.i: If Athena of many plans grants me the glory of killing both,
sentences.n: αἴ κέν is εἰ κέν ‘if ever’, with the aorist subjunctive ὀρέξῃ ‘should grant’ (κῦδος ὀρέξῃ ‘grant glory’). πολύβουλος ‘of many plans’ is built from πολύς and βουλή ‘plan’. ἀμφοτέρω is dual ‘both’, and the infinitive κτεῖναι says what the glory is, ‘to kill both’. The conditional clause stops at the comma; its answer is a set of instructions to Sthenelus, put as infinitives (the construction goes on to 264).

sentences.t:
σὺ δὲ τούσδε μὲν ὠκέας ἵππους
αὐτοῦ ἐρυκακέειν ἐξ ἄντυγος ἡνία τείνας,
Αἰνείαο δ’ ἐπαΐξαι μεμνημένος ἵππων,
ἐκ δ’ ἐλάσαι Τρώων μετ’ ἐϋκνήμιδας Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.tr:
sy de tousde men ōkeas hippous
autou erykakeein ex antygos hēnia teinas,
Aineiao d’ epaïxai memnēmenos hippōn,
ek d’ elasai Trōōn met’ eÿknēmidas Achaious.
sentences.l:
you these swift horses
here to hold back, the reins from the rail having stretched,
and at Aeneas’ horses to dash, being mindful of them,
and to drive them out from the Trojans among the well-greaved Achaeans.
sentences.i: then you are to hold these swift horses back here, with the reins made fast to the chariot’s rail, and dash at Aeneas’ horses, keeping them in mind, and drive them out from the Trojans among the well-greaved Achaeans.
sentences.n: Three infinitives stand for commands (‘you are to …’): ἐρυκακέειν, the epic reduplicated aorist infinitive of ἐρύκω ‘hold back’; ἐπαΐξαι ‘to dash at’; and ἐλάσαι ‘to drive’. σὺ δέ … μέν sets the two teams apart, τούσδε ‘these’ (Diomedes’ own horses) against Αἰνείαο … ἵππων ‘Aeneas’ horses’, which take the genitive after μεμνημένος ‘mindful of’. ἐξ ἄντυγος ἡνία τείνας is ‘having stretched the reins from the rail’ (ἄντυξ is the rim of the chariot-body), that is, made fast so that the team stands. ἐπαΐξαι has no stated object, and the horses are understood. ἐϋκνήμιδας Ἀχαιούς ‘well-greaved Achaeans’ is the stock phrase.

sentences.t:
τῆς γάρ τοι γενεῆς ἧς Τρωΐ περ εὐρύοπα Ζεὺς
δῶχ’ υἷος ποινὴν Γανυμήδεος, οὕνεκ’ ἄριστοι
ἵππων ὅσσοι ἔασιν ὑπ’ ἠῶ τ’ ἠέλιόν τε,
sentences.tr:
tēs gar toi geneēs hēs Trōï per euryopa Zeus
dōch’ huios poinēn Ganymēdeos, hounek’ aristoi
hippōn hossoi easin hyp’ ēō t’ ēelion te,
sentences.l:
For of that breed which to Tros far-thundering Zeus
gave as requital for his son Ganymede, because the best
of horses, as many as there are beneath the dawn and the sun,
sentences.i: For of that breed which Zeus who thunders from afar gave to Tros as requital for his son Ganymede, because they are the best of all horses beneath the dawn and the sun,
sentences.n: τῆς … γενεῆς ‘of that breed’ begins a long sentence that is picked up in 268, where τῆς γενεῆς returns; the clause between explains why the breed matters. ἧς ‘which’ is a relative with Ζεὺς … δῶκε (δῶχ’ is δῶκε), and Τρωΐ is the dative of Τρώς, Tros, whose son Ganymede was taken by Zeus; the horses are Zeus’ payment (ποινή ‘requital’) to the father. υἷος is the epic genitive of υἱός. εὐρύοπα is Zeus’ epithet ‘far-thundering’, a traditional gloss whose second element is disputed. ὅσσοι ἔασιν ὑπ’ ἠῶ τ’ ἠέλιόν τε is ‘as many as there are under the dawn and the sun’, that is, anywhere in the world.

sentences.t:
τῆς γενεῆς ἔκλεψεν ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγχίσης
λάθρῃ Λαομέδοντος ὑποσχὼν θήλεας ἵππους·
sentences.tr:
tēs geneēs eklepsen anax andrōn Anchisēs
lathrēi Laomedontos hyposchōn thēleas hippous·
sentences.l:
from that breed stole the lord of men Anchises,
in secret from Laomedon, having put mares under.
sentences.i: Anchises, lord of men, stole from that breed, secretly from Laomedon, by putting mares under the stallions;
sentences.n: ἔκλεψεν ‘stole’ and its subject ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγχίσης ‘Anchises, lord of men’ complete the sentence opened in 265. λάθρῃ Λαομέδοντος is ‘secretly from Laomedon’, the king of Troy of that time, with a genitive of the person kept in ignorance. ὑποσχών is the aorist participle of ὑπέχω ‘put under’; the Greek names only θήλεας ἵππους ‘female horses’ (mares), and the stallions they were put under are understood, which is the usual way of taking it.

sentences.t: τῶν οἱ ἓξ ἐγένοντο ἐνὶ μεγάροισι γενέθλη.
sentences.tr: tōn hoi hex egenonto eni megaroisi genethlē.
sentences.l: Of these six for him were born in his halls, as offspring.
sentences.i: Six of these were born to him in his halls as his offspring.
sentences.n: τῶν οἱ ἓξ ἐγένοντο is ‘of these six were born to him’: τῶν points back to the stolen breed, and οἱ is ‘to him’ (Anchises). ἐνὶ μεγάροισι is ‘in the halls’, and γενέθλη ‘offspring’ (from γίγνομαι) stands in apposition to ἓξ. The next lines say what became of them.

sentences.t:
τοὺς μὲν τέσσαρας αὐτὸς ἔχων ἀτίταλλ’ ἐπὶ φάτνῃ,
τὼ δὲ δύ’ Αἰνείᾳ δῶκεν μήστωρε φόβοιο.
sentences.tr:
tous men tessaras autos echōn atitall’ epi phatnēi,
tō de dy’ Aineiāi dōken mēstōre phoboio.
sentences.l:
Of these the four, himself keeping them, he reared at the manger,
and the two he gave to Aeneas, counsellors of flight.
sentences.i: Four of them he kept himself and reared at the manger, and the other two he gave to Aeneas, masters of flight.
sentences.n: τοὺς μὲν τέσσαρας … τὼ δὲ δύ’ sets four against two, and ἔχων ἀτίταλλ’ is ‘kept and reared’ (the imperfect of ἀτιτάλλω ‘rear’, elided). ἐπὶ φάτνῃ is ‘at the manger’. τὼ … δύ’ is dual, ‘the two’, and μήστωρε is the dual of μήστωρ ‘counsellor, deviser’ (the same noun as in μήστωρες ἀϋτῆς, ‘masters of the battle-cry’, 4.328), here with φόβοιο ‘of flight’: horses that know how to run. Αἰνείᾳ is the dative of Αἰνείας.

sentences.t: εἰ τούτω κε λάβοιμεν, ἀροίμεθά κε κλέος ἐσθλόν.
sentences.tr: ei toutō ke laboimen, aroimetha ke kleos esthlon.
sentences.l: If these two we could take, we should win good glory.”
sentences.i: If we could take these two, we should win good glory.”
sentences.n: εἰ … κε λάβοιμεν is ‘if we could take’, the aorist optative of λαμβάνω, with ἀροίμεθά κε, the aorist optative middle of ἄρνυμαι ‘win’, as its answer; τούτω is dual, ‘these two (horses)’. κλέος ἐσθλόν is ‘good glory’. Diomedes’ speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἳ μὲν τοιαῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀγόρευον,
τὼ δὲ τάχ’ ἐγγύθεν ἦλθον ἐλαύνοντ’ ὠκέας ἵππους.
sentences.tr:
hōs hoi men toiauta pros allēlous agoreuon,
tō de tach’ engythen ēlthon elaunont’ ōkeas hippous.
sentences.l:
So they, on the one hand, such things to one another were speaking,
and the two soon came near, driving the swift horses.
sentences.i: So they spoke such words to one another, and the two soon came near, driving their swift horses.
sentences.n: ὣς οἳ μέν … τὼ δέ turns from Diomedes and Sthenelus (οἵ ‘they’) to Aeneas and Pandarus (τώ, the dual ‘those two’). ἀγόρευον is the imperfect of ἀγορεύω ‘speak’, ἐγγύθεν is ‘from near, close by’, τάχα ‘soon’, and ἐλαύνοντ’ is the dual participle of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’. A new paragraph begins at 274.

sentences.t: τὸν πρότερος προσέειπε Λυκάονος ἀγλαὸς υἱός·
sentences.tr: ton proteros proseeipe Lykaonos aglaos huios·
sentences.l: Him first addressed Lycaon’s splendid son:
sentences.i: Lycaon’s splendid son spoke to him first:
sentences.n: τόν ‘him’ is Diomedes. πρότερος ‘first’ is an adjective used where English has an adverb, and it says that Pandarus speaks before Diomedes can. Λυκάονος ἀγλαὸς υἱός ‘Lycaon’s splendid son’ is Pandarus, and προσέειπε the aorist of προσεῖπον ‘address’.

sentences.t:
καρτερόθυμε δαΐφρον ἀγαυοῦ Τυδέος υἱὲ
ἦ μάλα σ’ οὐ βέλος ὠκὺ δαμάσσατο πικρὸς ὀϊστός·
sentences.tr:
karterothyme daïphron agauou Tydeos huie
ē mala s’ ou belos ōky damassato pikros oïstos·
sentences.l:
“Strong-hearted, wise-minded son of noble Tydeus,
truly the swift shaft did not subdue you, the bitter arrow;
sentences.i: “Strong-hearted and wise-hearted son of noble Tydeus, truly the swift shaft, the bitter arrow, did not overcome you;
sentences.n: καρτερόθυμε and δαΐφρον are vocatives agreeing with υἱέ ‘son’: καρτερόθυμος ‘strong-hearted’ is built from καρτερός and θυμός, and δαΐφρων ‘wise-hearted’ is a stock epithet whose sense (‘wise’ or ‘fierce’) is disputed. ἀγαυοῦ ‘noble’ goes with Τυδέος. ἦ μάλα is ‘truly’, with σε as the object of δαμάσσατο, the aorist middle of δαμάζω ‘subdue’ (used like an active). βέλος ὠκύ is ‘the swift shaft’ and πικρὸς ὀϊστός ‘the bitter arrow’ is in apposition to it; Pandarus is speaking of his earlier shot at Diomedes’ shoulder. The tone is mocking.

sentences.t: νῦν αὖτ’ ἐγχείῃ πειρήσομαι αἴ κε τύχωμι.
sentences.tr: nyn aut’ encheiēi peirēsomai ai ke tychōmi.
sentences.l: now in turn with a spear I will make trial, if I may hit.”
sentences.i: now I will try with my spear, to see if I can hit you.”
sentences.n: νῦν αὖτ’ is ‘now in turn’ (αὖτε ‘again, in turn’), picking up the arrow with the spear. ἐγχείῃ is the dative ‘with a spear’, πειρήσομαι is ‘I will make trial’, and αἴ κε τύχωμι is ‘if I may hit’ (αἴ κε = εἰ κε, and τύχωμι the aorist subjunctive of τυγχάνω with the old ending -μι). Pandarus’ speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα καὶ ἀμπεπαλὼν προΐει δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος
καὶ βάλε Τυδεΐδαο κατ’ ἀσπίδα·
sentences.tr:
ē rha kai ampepalōn proïei dolichoskion enchos
kai bale Tydeïdao kat’ aspida·
sentences.l:
He spoke, and having brandished it he sent forth his long-shadowed spear,
and hit the son of Tydeus on the shield;
sentences.i: So he said, and brandishing it he sent forth his long-shadowed spear, and hit the son of Tydeus on his shield;
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα καί is ‘he spoke, and’; ἀμπεπαλών is the aorist participle of ἀναπάλλω ‘swing back, brandish’; and προΐει δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος is ‘sent forth the long-shadowed spear’, the same words as for other casts. βάλε is the unaugmented aorist ‘hit’, and Τυδεΐδαο, the epic genitive of Τυδεΐδης, is ‘the son of Tydeus’. A new paragraph begins at 280.

sentences.t:
τῆς δὲ διὰ πρὸ
αἰχμὴ χαλκείη πταμένη θώρηκι πελάσθη·
sentences.tr:
tēs de dia pro
aichmē chalkeiē ptamenē thōrēki pelasthē·
sentences.l:
and through it, on,
the bronze point, flying, was brought near to the breastplate;
sentences.i: and the bronze point flew right through it and came up against the breastplate;
sentences.n: τῆς is ‘it’, the shield, and διὰ πρό is διαπρό ‘right through’, with τῆς put before it, followed by πταμένη, the aorist participle of πέτομαι ‘flying’. αἰχμὴ χαλκείη is ‘the bronze point’. πελάσθη is the aorist passive of πελάζω ‘bring near’ with the dative θώρηκι ‘to the breastplate’: the point reaches the breastplate and goes no further.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ ἐπὶ μακρὸν ἄϋσε Λυκάονος ἀγλαὸς υἱός·
sentences.tr: tōi d’ epi makron aÿse Lykaonos aglaos huios·
sentences.l: and over him shouted loudly Lycaon’s splendid son:
sentences.i: and over him Lycaon’s splendid son cried out loudly:
sentences.n: τῷ δ’ ἐπί is ‘and over him’, and μακρὸν ἄϋσε ‘shouted loudly’ is a stock phrase, with μακρόν an adverb ‘long, loud’ and ἄϋσε an unaugmented aorist. The shout is a boast over a man he thinks he has hit, and it fills the next two lines.

sentences.t:
βέβληαι κενεῶνα διαμπερές, οὐδέ σ’ ὀΐω
δηρὸν ἔτ’ ἀνσχήσεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
beblēai keneōna diamperes, oude s’ oïō
dēron et’ anschēsesthai·
sentences.l:
“You are hit in the flank right through, and I do not think you
will long yet hold out;
sentences.i: “You are hit right through the flank, and I do not think you will hold out much longer;
sentences.n: βέβληαι is the perfect passive of βάλλω, ‘you stand hit’, with κενεῶνα ‘in the flank’ (the soft part below the ribs) as an accusative of the place struck, and διαμπερές ‘right through’. The claim is wrong: the point stopped at the breastplate (282), and Diomedes says so. οὐδέ σ’ ὀΐω is ‘nor do I think you’, with the future infinitive ἀνσχήσεσθαι ‘will hold out’ and δηρὸν ἔτ’ ‘for long yet’.

sentences.t: ἐμοὶ δὲ μέγ’ εὖχος ἔδωκας.
sentences.tr: emoi de meg’ euchos edōkas.
sentences.l: and to me a great boast you have given.”
sentences.i: and you have given me great cause to boast.”
sentences.n: εὖχος is something to boast of, the claim to a great kill; ἔδωκας ‘you have given’ is an aorist of δίδωμι. Pandarus’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ οὐ ταρβήσας προσέφη κρατερὸς Διομήδης·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ou tarbēsas prosephē krateros Diomēdēs·
sentences.l: Him then, not terrified, addressed strong Diomedes:
sentences.i: Then strong Diomedes, unafraid, spoke to him:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ … προσέφη κρατερὸς Διομήδης is the reply formula of 251 with οὐ ταρβήσας ‘not having been afraid’ in place of the scowl; ταρβήσας is the aorist participle of ταρβέω ‘be afraid’. A new paragraph begins at 286.

sentences.t: ἤμβροτες οὐδ’ ἔτυχες·
sentences.tr: ēmbrotes oud’ etyches·
sentences.l: “You missed and did not hit;
sentences.i: “You missed and did not hit;
sentences.n: ἤμβροτες is the aorist of ἁμαρτάνω ‘miss’, and οὐδ’ ἔτυχες ‘and did not hit’ is the aorist of τυγχάνω; both verbs lack an object, and the sense is that the cast went astray. Diomedes’ answer to the boast opens with the plain fact.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ οὐ μὲν σφῶΐ γ’ ὀΐω
πρίν γ’ ἀποπαύσεσθαι πρίν γ’ ἢ ἕτερόν γε πεσόντα
αἵματος ἆσαι Ἄρηα, ταλαύρινον πολεμιστήν.
sentences.tr:
atar ou men sphōï g’ oïō
prin g’ apopausesthai prin g’ ē heteron ge pesonta
haimatos asai Arēa, talaurinon polemistēn.
sentences.l:
but not indeed you two, I think,
will cease before, before one of the two at least, having fallen,
has glutted with blood Ares, the shield-enduring warrior.”
sentences.i: But I do not think you two will stop before one or the other has fallen and glutted Ares, the warrior who bears the hide shield, with his blood.”
sentences.n: ἀτὰρ οὐ μέν … γ’ ὀΐω is ‘but truly I do not think’, with σφῶϊ ‘you two’ (the dual pronoun) as the subject of the future infinitive ἀποπαύσεσθαι ‘will stop’; the second πρίν restates the first, ‘not before … before …’. ἕτερόν γε πεσόντα ‘one of the two having fallen’ is the subject of ἆσαι, the aorist infinitive of ἄω ‘satiate’, with αἵματος ‘with blood’. Ἄρηα is the god himself, called ταλαύρινος, a compound of an element meaning ‘endure’ and ῥινός ‘hide’, so ‘enduring the hide shield’ (the sense is the traditional one), and πολεμιστής ‘warrior’. Diomedes’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς φάμενος προέηκε·
sentences.tr: hōs phamenos proeēke·
sentences.l: So saying, he sent it forth;
sentences.i: With these words he sent his spear forth;
sentences.n: ὣς φάμενος is ‘so saying’ (φάμενος the participle of φημί), and προέηκε the aorist of προΐημι ‘send forth’, the same verb as προΐει at 280; the object, the spear, is left to be understood. The next lines show where it goes. A new paragraph begins at 290.

sentences.t:
βέλος δ’ ἴθυνεν Ἀθήνη
ῥῖνα παρ’ ὀφθαλμόν, λευκοὺς δ’ ἐπέρησεν ὀδόντας.
sentences.tr:
belos d’ ithynen Athēnē
rhina par’ ophthalmon, leukous d’ eperēsen odontas.
sentences.l:
and the shaft Athena guided straight
to the nose beside the eye, and the white teeth it pierced.
sentences.i: and Athena guided the shaft straight to the nose beside the eye, and it pierced the white teeth.
sentences.n: βέλος ‘shaft’ is Diomedes’ spear, and Athena is its guide (ἴθυνεν ‘made straight’, from ἰθύς ‘straight’). ῥῖνα παρ’ ὀφθαλμόν is ‘to the nose beside the eye’. ἐπέρησεν is the aorist of περάω ‘pierce through’, and λευκοὺς … ὀδόντας ‘the white teeth’. The man hit is Pandarus, though the narrator does not name him.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ ἀπὸ μὲν γλῶσσαν πρυμνὴν τάμε χαλκὸς ἀτειρής,
αἰχμὴ δ’ ἐξελύθη παρὰ νείατον ἀνθερεῶνα·
sentences.tr:
tou d’ apo men glōssan prymnēn tame chalkos ateirēs,
aichmē d’ exelythē para neiaton anthereōna·
sentences.l:
and from him the tongue at its root cut the unwearied bronze,
and the point was released beside the lowest part of the chin;
sentences.i: The unwearied bronze cut his tongue off at the root, and the point came out beside the lowest part of the chin;
sentences.n: τοῦ … ἀπὸ … τάμε is ἀπέτεμε ‘cut off’ with the preverb split from its verb (tmesis) and τοῦ ‘from him’. γλῶσσαν πρυμνήν is ‘the tongue at its root’ (πρυμνός ‘hindmost, at the base’). χαλκὸς ἀτειρής is ‘the unwearied bronze’, an epithet that is the same every time (ἀτειρής from ἀ- and τείρω ‘wear down’). ἐξελύθη is the aorist passive of ἐκλύω ‘loose’, so ‘came loose out’; νείατον ἀνθερεῶνα is ‘the lowest part of the chin’ (νείατος ‘lowest’).

sentences.t:
ἤριπε δ’ ἐξ ὀχέων, ἀράβησε δὲ τεύχε’ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ
αἰόλα παμφανόωντα, παρέτρεσσαν δέ οἱ ἵπποι
ὠκύποδες·
sentences.tr:
ēripe d’ ex ocheōn, arabēse de teuche’ ep’ autōi
aiola pamphanoōnta, paretressan de hoi hippoi
ōkypodes·
sentences.i: He crashed down from his chariot, and his armour clattered upon him, glancing and all-shining, and the swift-footed horses shied away from him;
sentences.n: The subject is the man just hit. ἤριπε is the aorist of ἐρείπω ‘crash down’, and ἀράβησε δὲ τεύχε’ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ is ‘and his armour clattered upon him’ (τεύχεα, elided). αἰόλα ‘glancing’ is the traditional rendering of an adjective whose sense (quick-moving or gleaming) is not known; παμφανόωντα is ‘all-shining’. παρέτρεσσαν is the aorist of παρατρέω ‘shy aside’, with οἱ ‘from him’, and ὠκύποδες is ‘swift-footed’ (ὠκύς + πούς), a stock epithet of horses.

sentences.t: τοῦ δ’ αὖθι λύθη ψυχή τε μένος τε.
sentences.tr: tou d’ authi lythē psychē te menos te.
sentences.l: and of him on the spot was loosed the soul and the might.
sentences.i: and on the spot his soul and his might were loosed.
sentences.n: τοῦ δ’ is ‘and of him’, αὖθι ‘on the spot’, and λύθη is the aorist passive of λύω ‘loose’, with ψυχή ‘soul’ and μένος ‘might’ as its two subjects: the dead man’s life, and the strength that drove him, leave together. The soul is what departs the body for Hades (as in the poem’s first lines).

sentences.t:
Αἰνείας δ’ ἀπόρουσε σὺν ἀσπίδι δουρί τε μακρῷ
δείσας μή πώς οἱ ἐρυσαίατο νεκρὸν Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.tr:
Aineias d’ aporouse syn aspidi douri te makrōi
deisas mē pōs hoi erysaiato nekron Achaioi.
sentences.l:
And Aeneas leapt down with shield and long spear,
afraid lest in some way for him they should drag off the corpse, the Achaeans.
sentences.i: Aeneas leapt down with his shield and long spear, afraid that the Achaeans might somehow drag the corpse away.
sentences.n: ἀπόρουσε is the aorist of ἀποθρῴσκω ‘leap off’, and Aeneas leaves his chariot. σὺν ἀσπίδι δουρί τε μακρῷ is ‘with shield and long spear’. δείσας μή πως … is ‘afraid lest in some way …’: ἐρυσαίατο is the aorist optative middle of ἐρύω ‘drag’ (-αίατο for -αῖντο), and οἱ ‘for him’ looks to the dead man, Pandarus, whose body is the νεκρόν. A new paragraph begins at 297.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρ’ αὐτῷ βαῖνε λέων ὣς ἀλκὶ πεποιθώς,
πρόσθε δέ οἱ δόρυ τ’ ἔσχε καὶ ἀσπίδα πάντοσ’ ἐΐσην,
τὸν κτάμεναι μεμαὼς ὅς τις τοῦ γ’ ἀντίος ἔλθοι
σμερδαλέα ἰάχων·
sentences.tr:
amphi d’ ar’ autōi baine leōn hōs alki pepoithōs,
prosthe de hoi dory t’ esche kai aspida pantos’ eïsēn,
ton ktamenai memaōs hos tis tou g’ antios elthoi
smerdalea iachōn·
sentences.l:
And around him he strode like a lion trusting in his might,
and before him held both spear and shield equal on every side,
eager to kill the man who against him might come,
terribly crying out;
sentences.i: He strode round him like a lion that trusts in its might, and held his spear and his shield, equal on every side, in front of him, eager to kill whoever might come against him, crying out terribly;
sentences.n: ἀμφὶ … βαῖνε is ‘strode about’ (tmesis again), with αὐτῷ ‘him’, the corpse, so Aeneas bestrides it to guard it. λέων ὣς is ‘like a lion’ (ὥς after its noun), and ἀλκὶ πεποιθώς is ‘trusting in his might’ (ἀλκί is a dative of ἀλκή, and πεποιθώς the perfect participle of πείθομαι ‘trust’). πάντοσ’ ἐΐσην is ‘equal on every side’, the same epithet as for the round shield elsewhere. τὸν κτάμεναι μεμαώς ὅς τις … ἔλθοι is ‘eager to kill the man who should come’ (κτάμεναι is the epic infinitive of κτείνω, and ἔλθοι an optative of the indefinite kind), and σμερδαλέα, a neuter plural used as an adverb, ‘terribly’, goes with ἰάχων ‘crying out’.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ χερμάδιον λάβε χειρὶ
Τυδεΐδης μέγα ἔργον ὃ οὐ δύο γ’ ἄνδρε φέροιεν,
οἷοι νῦν βροτοί εἰσ’·
sentences.tr:
ho de chermadion labe cheiri
Tydeïdēs mega ergon ho ou dyo g’ andre pheroien,
hoioi nyn brotoi eis’·
sentences.i: And the son of Tydeus took in his hand a rock, a great piece of work, one that two men, such as mortals now are, could not carry;
sentences.n: ὃ δέ ‘and he’ is Diomedes (Τυδεΐδης follows in 303), and χερμάδιον is a hand-sized missile, here a rock too heavy for two ordinary men. μέγα ἔργον ‘a great work’ is in apposition to the rock, a thing that is hard labour to move. ὃ οὐ δύο γ’ ἄνδρε φέροιεν is ‘which two men could not carry’ (ἄνδρε is dual, and φέροιεν a potential optative), and οἷοι νῦν βροτοί εἰσ’ is ‘such as mortals now are’: the poet says that men of his time are weaker than the men of the story.

sentences.t: ὃ δέ μιν ῥέα πάλλε καὶ οἶος.
sentences.tr: ho de min rhea palle kai oios.
sentences.l: but he easily swung it, and alone.
sentences.i: but he swung it easily, even alone.
sentences.n: ὃ δέ ‘but he’ sets Diomedes against the two men of the day, and μιν is the rock. ῥέα is ‘easily’, πάλλε the imperfect of πάλλω ‘swing’, and οἶος ‘alone, by himself’.

sentences.t:
τῷ βάλεν Αἰνείαο κατ’ ἰσχίον ἔνθά τε μηρὸς
ἰσχίῳ ἐνστρέφεται, κοτύλην δέ τέ μιν καλέουσι·
sentences.tr:
tōi balen Aineiao kat’ ischion entha te mēros
ischiōi enstrephetai, kotylēn de te min kaleousi·
sentences.l:
With it he hit Aeneas on the hip, where the thigh
turns in the hip, and cup they call it;
sentences.i: With it he hit Aeneas on the hip, where the thigh turns in the hip, the place that people call the cup;
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘with it’ (the rock). Αἰνείαο is the epic genitive and κατ’ ἰσχίον ‘on the hip’ the place hit; ἔνθά τε μηρὸς ἰσχίῳ ἐνστρέφεται is ‘where the thigh turns in the hip’, the hip-joint, which gets a name: κοτύλη means ‘cup’, and here is the socket of the hip. κοτύλην δέ τέ μιν καλέουσι is ‘and a cup they call it’.

sentences.t: θλάσσε δέ οἱ κοτύλην, πρὸς δ’ ἄμφω ῥῆξε τένοντε·
sentences.tr: thlasse de hoi kotylēn, pros d’ amphō rhēxe tenonte·
sentences.l: and crushed for him the cup, and besides both tendons it broke;
sentences.i: and crushed his cup, and broke both tendons besides;
sentences.n: The subject is the rock, not stated. θλάσσε is the unaugmented aorist of θλάω ‘crush’, οἱ ‘for him’, κοτύλην ‘the cup’ (see 306), and πρὸς δ’ … ῥῆξε is ‘and besides … broke’, with τένοντε the dual ‘two tendons’ of the joint, and ἄμφω ‘both’.

sentences.t: ὦσε δ’ ἀπὸ ῥινὸν τρηχὺς λίθος·
sentences.tr: ōse d’ apo rhinon trēchys lithos·
sentences.l: and pushed off the skin the rough stone;
sentences.i: and the rough stone shoved the skin away;
sentences.n: ὦσε is the unaugmented aorist of ὠθέω ‘push’, ῥινόν the accusative of ῥινός ‘skin, hide’ (the plural ῥινοί was ‘hides’ in the shields at 4.447), and τρηχὺς λίθος ‘the rough stone’ is the subject, held back to the end of the clause. The skin torn away is Aeneas’ own.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ἥρως
ἔστη γνὺξ ἐριπὼν καὶ ἐρείσατο χειρὶ παχείῃ
γαίης·
sentences.tr:
autar ho g’ hērōs
estē gnyx eripōn kai ereisato cheiri pacheiēi
gaiēs·
sentences.i: But the hero crashed down, came to a stand on his knees, and propped himself with a stout hand on the ground;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ἥρως ‘but he, the hero’ is Aeneas. ἔστη γνὺξ ἐριπών is ‘stood on his knees, having crashed down’ (ἔστη the aorist of ἵστημι, γνύξ ‘on the knee’, ἐριπών the aorist participle of ἐρείπω), a man halfway to the ground. ἐρείσατο is the aorist middle of ἐρείδω ‘prop’, with χειρὶ παχείῃ ‘with a stout hand’ and the genitive γαίης ‘on the earth’.

sentences.t: ἀμφὶ δὲ ὄσσε κελαινὴ νὺξ ἐκάλυψε.
sentences.tr: amphi de osse kelainē nyx ekalypse.
sentences.l: and around his two eyes dark night covered.
sentences.i: and dark night covered his eyes.
sentences.n: ἀμφὶ … ἐκάλυψε is ‘covered around’, the preverb split from its verb, and ὄσσε is dual ‘the two eyes’. κελαινὴ νύξ ‘dark night’ is the sign that he is fainting, and Aeneas is fainting, not dead.

sentences.t:
καί νύ κεν ἔνθ’ ἀπόλοιτο ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Αἰνείας,
εἰ μὴ ἄρ’ ὀξὺ νόησε Διὸς θυγάτηρ Ἀφροδίτη
μήτηρ, ἥ μιν ὑπ’ Ἀγχίσῃ τέκε βουκολέοντι·
sentences.tr:
kai ny ken enth’ apoloito anax andrōn Aineias,
ei mē ar’ oxy noēse Dios thygatēr Aphroditē
mētēr, hē min hyp’ Anchisēi teke boukoleonti·
sentences.i: And now Aeneas, lord of men, would have perished there, had Aphrodite, the daughter of Zeus, not been quick to notice, his mother, who bore him to Anchises while he tended cattle;
sentences.n: καί νύ κεν … ἀπόλοιτο is ‘and now he would have perished’, a potential optative of ἀπόλλυμι in the story’s past. εἰ μὴ ἄρ’ ὀξὺ νόησε ‘if she had not sharply noticed’ is a whole line already used in Aphrodite’s rescue of Paris (3.374), repeated for her rescue of her son; Διὸς θυγάτηρ is ‘daughter of Zeus’. ἥ μιν ὑπ’ Ἀγχίσῃ τέκε βουκολέοντι is ‘who bore him to Anchises, as he tended cattle’ (βουκολέοντι is a dative participle, from βουκολέω). A new paragraph begins at 311.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἑὸν φίλον υἱὸν ἐχεύατο πήχεε λευκώ,
πρόσθε δέ οἱ πέπλοιο φαεινοῦ πτύγμα κάλυψεν
ἕρκος ἔμεν βελέων, μή τις Δαναῶν ταχυπώλων
χαλκὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσι βαλὼν ἐκ θυμὸν ἕλοιτο.
sentences.tr:
amphi d’ heon philon huion echeuato pēchee leukō,
prosthe de hoi peploio phaeinou ptygma kalypsen
herkos emen beleōn, mē tis Danaōn tachypōlōn
chalkon eni stēthessi balōn ek thymon heloito.
sentences.l:
Around her dear son she poured her two white arms,
and in front of him a fold of her shining robe covered him
to be a fence against shafts, lest any of the swift-colted Danaans,
having cast bronze in his chest, should take his life from him.
sentences.i: She threw her white arms about her dear son, and in front of him a fold of her shining robe covered him, to be a bulwark against shafts, lest any of the Danaans with their swift colts strike bronze into his chest and take his life.
sentences.n: ἀμφί … ἐχεύατο is ‘she poured around’ (the aorist middle of χέω, with the preverb split off), and πήχεε λευκώ is the dual ‘two white arms’. ἑὸν φίλον υἱόν is ‘her own dear son’ (ἑός is the possessive ‘own’). The syntax of πρόσθε δέ οἱ πέπλοιο φαεινοῦ πτύγμα κάλυψεν has the fold as the subject of κάλυψεν ‘covered’, with ‘him’ understood; πτύγμα is ‘fold’, φαεινός ‘shining’. ἕρκος ἔμεν βελέων is ‘to be a fence against shafts’ (ἔμεν = εἶναι), with μή τις … ἕλοιτο ‘lest any … take’, and Δαναῶν ταχυπώλων ‘of the Danaans with swift colts’. χαλκὸν … βαλών is ‘having cast bronze’, the weapon for its point, and ἐκ θυμὸν ἕλοιτο ‘take out his life’ (ἐκ is split from ἕλοιτο).
